what: Bell Labs (Balashek, Biddulph, Davis) built Audrey, a single-speaker spoken-digit recognizer: a machine sense of hearing.

sources.title: Speech recognition
sources.quote: 1952 - Bell Labs researchers, Stephen Balashek, R. Biddulph, and K. H. Davis, built Audrey for single-speaker digit recognition.

note: Definition includes hearing, so Audrey (1952) precedes the 1982 e-nose start by 30 years. Weakness: Audrey recognised only digits from one speaker, so 'comparable to a person' is loose. Looked for earlier smell/touch/taste: Moncrieff 1961 odour sensor and 1960s tactile arrays are later than 1952 and could not be sourced; Wikipedia Electronic nose says real progress on odour measurement came only in the 1950s or later; Bach-y-Rita 1960s tactile display is later and is a display, not a machine sense.

what: Griffith P. Taylor built a Meccano programmable crane robot (punched-tape controlled, five axes) that stacked blocks; published in Meccano Magazine, March 1938.

sources.title: Industrial robot
sources.quote: The earliest known industrial robot conforming to the ISO definition was completed by

note: Looked for earlier programmable arm/machine: Devol patent 1954 and Unimate prototypes late 1950s are later; Roselund/DeVilbiss spray-painting patents (1938-42) later and unsourced. Taylor 1937 Meccano crane is a working programmable (punched-tape, five-axis) machine, which fits 'shown to work', though a hobby model; no earlier working one found.

what: First Unimate installed at GM Inland Fisher Guide plant, Ewing Township NJ, lifting hot die-cast parts.

sources.title: Unimate
sources.quote: which worked on a General Motors assembly line at the Inland Fisher Guide Plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, in 1961

sources.title: Unimation
sources.quote: In 1960, Devol personally sold the first Unimate robot, which was shipped in 1961 to General Motors.

note: Unimate shipped 1961 to GM Inland Fisher Guide, Ewing NJ, per Wikipedia (Unimation/Unimate). Claimed 1959 Trenton prototype not found in any fetchable source (Wikipedia Unimate has no mention). Earlier painting-robot patents had no verified deployment.

what: Fanuc's robot plant near Mount Fuji runs lights-out, robots building robots, unsupervised for up to 30 days.

sources.title: Lights out (manufacturing)
sources.quote: FANUC, a Japanese robotics company, has been a lights-out factory since 2001.

note: Searched for earlier unmanned plants. Press (Christian Science Monitor 15 Apr 1981) reportedly describes Fujitsu Fanuc's Yamanashi robot plant run by robots 16 hours a day from 1981, but csmonitor.com is blocked here so the quote could not be verified; it was also not fully unmanned. Molins System 24 (1960s) unsourced and not a self-maintaining plant. Kept 2001 on the only verified source; likely too late, so a human should re-check the 1981 report.

what: Sony introduced the first consumer AIBO robot dog (ERS-110)

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: The first consumer model was introduced on 11 May 1999 and was followed by updated generations.

note: Earlier: Elektro/Sparko 1939-40 are exhibits, Paro designed from 1993 but first public in 2001, Furby 1998 is a toy creature not a companion. No earlier robot built for companionship found. Companionship fit of AIBO is loose.

what: AIBO ERS-110 went on sale and sold out in 20 minutes

sources.title: AIBO
sources.quote: Sales began on 1 June 1999 and sold out via the Internet in 20 minutes.

note: Earlier: Paro handmade sales from 2004, Furby 1998 is a pet toy, not marketed as companion robot; no earlier sale of a companion robot found.

what: Ideal Toy Company sold Gaylord, a battery-powered toy dog steered by its leash.

sources.title: Robot dog
sources.quote: Gaylord (Ideal Toy Company), robotic dog controllable by leash, produced in the 1960s

note: Wikipedia's Robot dog list gives only 'the 1960s'; the year 1962 comes from a web-search summary of toytales.ca (page blocked, not fetched), so date is unverified within the decade. Gaylord is a motorised toy dog, arguably mechanical rather than robotic. Rejected: Sparko 1940 (exhibit, never sold, per Wikipedia Robotic pet), Teddy Ruxpin 1985 (bear, not a pet animal).

what: Furby sold 14 million units in 1999 after 1.8 million in 1998

sources.title: Furby
sources.quote: with 1.8 million sold in 1998 and 14 million in 1999

note: Gaylord (1960s) was a small-scale toy, no sales figures found; Furby's 14 million in 1999 is the first documented mass sale of pet-like toys. AIBO sold only thousands.

what: Knightscope shipped its first autonomous security patrol robot

sources.title: Knightscope
sources.quote: Knightscope shipped their first robot in 2015.

note: Knightscope 2015 is probably late. Earlier: Denning Sentry, introduced 1985 per Computer History Museum ('designed this robot as a security guard patrolling for up to 14 hours'), but CHM says the product did not succeed and press said none were sold, so practical use is not shown; Cybermotion SR2 at LACMA, ROBART and PROWLER could not be dated or sourced. A human should look for first deployed Cybermotion/Denning units.

what: Walgreens installed a Kiva mobile-robot fulfilment system at Mount Vernon, Illinois

sources.title: Amazon Robotics
sources.quote: Walgreens installed one at its distribution center in Mount Vernon, Illinois, in 2007

note: Possibly too late: wire-guided AGV fleets (Volvo Kalmar 1972-74, Tetra Pak Lund 1976 with 20 AGVs and a control system per Wikipedia NDC) existed earlier, but no fetchable source states a central computer directing them, so not substituted. Staples 2006 not confirmed.

what: Parrot unveiled the AR.Drone at CES 2010, a smartphone-controlled consumer quadcopter; about half a million AR.Drones had been sold by early 2013.

sources.title: Parrot AR.Drone
sources.quote: The Parrot AR.Drone was unveiled at the International CES 2010 in Las Vegas along with a demonstration of the iOS applications used to control it.

sources.title: Parrot AR.Drone
sources.quote: By early 2013, around half a million units of the AR.Drone and its successor had been sold.

note: AR.Drone predates the DJI Phantom (2013) as a mass-market consumer drone; the 500,000 figure spans 2010 to early 2013, so scale in 2010 itself is not shown. Hobby RC model aircraft (1960s on) rejected: not the scout/carry/attack drone of the definition. Phantom said to have captured the consumer market, which is the later, bigger step.

what: J. Lyons & Co's LEO I computer, in business use from 1951, calculated bakery and tea-shop overnight production requirements and delivery schedules from daily shop orders.

sources.title: LEO (computer)
sources.quote: calculate the overnight production requirements, assembly instructions, delivery schedules, invoices, costings, and management reports.

note: Computers planning production for a firm predate Cybersyn (1971-73) by 20 years, but this is firm-level, not economy-level, and the page gives no date for the production-planning job (LEO I's first business job, Bakery Valuations, ran 5 September 1951; the orders job was an 'early task'), so 1951 is an approximate bound. USAF Project SCOOP (c.1951) and NYSE DOT (1970s) could not be sourced. Cybersyn's own use is dated October 1972 only by one page, and the prototype stage was 1972.
